provenance.authorship: Original project scenario, AI-assisted draft. Practitioner review and scoring calibration pending.

title: Explain a Career Change
prompt: Practice explaining a move into a different type of work. Choose a target role and state up to two duties you know it involves, or use this fictional fallback: a coordinator who tracks requests and communicates handoffs. Explain how one experience you already have could help, and one skill you would still need to learn. You may use paid work, study, informal work, volunteering, or military experience.
blurb: Turn existing experience into credible evidence for a new field without pretending the roles are identical.

rubric.label: Transferable skill
rubric.description: Connects a past action to a target duty.

anchors.0: Claims every skill transfers without explaining a connection.
anchors.2: Links one past action to one target duty.
anchors.4: Explains both the useful similarity and a meaningful difference between the settings.

rubric.label: Personal evidence
rubric.description: Describes what they contributed and the outcome.

anchors.0: Takes credit for work their account attributes entirely to others.
anchors.2: Identifies an action they took and an outcome.
anchors.4: Explains a decision, their contribution, and evidence of the outcome without overstating causality.

rubric.label: Credible learning plan
rubric.description: Identifies a gap and a way to address it.

anchors.0: Claims no learning is needed despite an identified gap.
anchors.2: Names a relevant gap and practice step.
anchors.4: Proposes a realistic practice step and a check that would show progress.

reference.scenario: Practice explaining a move into a different type of work. Choose a target role and state up to two duties you know it involves, or use this fictional fallback: a coordinator who tracks requests and communicates handoffs. Explain how one experience you already have could help, and one skill you would still need to learn. You may use paid work, study, informal work, volunteering, or military experience.

facts.value: The fallback coordinator uses a shared task list and gives a daily handoff; system training is provided.
facts.reveal_when: candidate chooses the fallback and asks about tools

facts.value: The fictional hiring manager accepts relevant examples from any setting; a prior coordinator title is not required.

model_points: A career change is not itself a weakness.
Translate evidence into duties, not merely job titles.
Distinguish demonstrated skills from skills the candidate plans to learn.

probes.trigger: candidate relies on jargon from the previous role
probes.question: How would you explain that contribution to someone outside your previous field?
What would be different about applying that skill in your target role?

red_flags: Invents qualifications, accomplishments, or employer commitments.
Uses unsupported assumptions about the candidate instead of job-related evidence.

interviewer_notes: Use only supplied role facts and candidate-provided experience. Accept examples from study, volunteering, caregiving, military service, informal work, and paid work without ranking their prestige. Do not demand disclosure of health, family, age, nationality, salary history, or reasons for a career gap. Do not score accent, appearance, eye contact, or native-like grammar. A hypothetical example must be identified as hypothetical, not passed off as experience. Missing evidence is not assessed, not automatically scored zero. In simulation ask neutral probes without giving a model answer; coaching may provide graduated help. Use only the duties the candidate supplies for their chosen target; say when other requirements are unknown. Do not invent hiring requirements or promise an employment outcome.

learning_drills.title: Make a transfer map
learning_drills.prompt: Create two rows pairing a previous action with a target duty; then add one gap and a small practice plan. This is self-guided practice; no model assessment is performed.
